notes.front: What is authorization?
notes.back: Deciding what an authenticated identity is allowed to do, and granting or denying access to specific resources.
notes.explanation: Authentication only confirms who you are; authorisation evaluates your permissions.
notes.example: Like a staff pass that opens the canteen and your own floor but not the server room.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define authentication and authorization, “Authorization”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is an identity provider (IdP)?
notes.back: A service that creates, maintains and manages identity information and offers authentication, authorisation and auditing services to applications.
notes.explanation: Applications hand these jobs to the identity provider instead of each keeping its own accounts and policies.
notes.example: Like a passport office that vouches for citizens, so each border post need not check birth records itself.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “The role of the identity provider”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a security token?
notes.back: A structured package of data that an identity provider issues after verifying a user’s identity.
notes.explanation: The application validates the token and uses what is inside it to grant access.
notes.example: Like a wristband a festival gate gives you after checking your ticket, which the stages then accept.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Security tokens and claims”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a security token, what is a claim?
notes.back: An individual piece of data about the authenticated identity, carried inside the token.
notes.explanation: Tokens carry their information in the form of claims.
notes.example: Like a single line on a boarding pass, such as the seat number or the passenger’s name.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Security tokens and claims”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is an ID token?
notes.back: A security token proving that the user has successfully signed in (authentication).
notes.explanation: The application uses it to know who the user is, such as their name, email and unique identifier.
notes.example: Like a visitor badge showing your name at reception, but it grants no keys to any room.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Security tokens and claims”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is an access token?
notes.back: A security token giving an application permission to access a specific resource on the user’s behalf (authorisation).
notes.explanation: It specifies what the application is allowed to do with that resource.
notes.example: Like a valet key that lets a car park attendant drive your car, but not open the boot.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Security tokens and claims”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is OAuth 2.0?
notes.back: An industry-standard protocol used for authorisation: it lets applications obtain access tokens to reach protected resources on the user’s behalf.
notes.explanation: It is one of the three most common protocols that identity providers and applications use.
notes.example: Like signing a form that lets a courier collect a parcel for you, without handing over your identity card.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Authentication protocols”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is OpenID Connect (OIDC)?
notes.back: A protocol widely used for authentication in modern cloud and mobile apps, letting them verify a user’s identity and get basic profile information.
notes.explanation: It is one of the three most common protocols the unit names.
notes.example: Like showing a photo card at a hotel desk so they know who you are, before any room is assigned.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Authentication protocols”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML)?
notes.back: A protocol commonly used in enterprise scenarios, especially for integrating older applications and for federation between organisations.
notes.explanation: The unit notes that it is often used with on-premises identity systems.
notes.example: Like a long-established letter of introduction format that older institutions still recognise.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Authentication protocols”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a directory service?
notes.back: Software that stores a directory, a structured repository of network objects such as users, devices and groups, and makes it available.
notes.explanation: The unit calls directory services the backbone of user authentication and authorisation in a network.
notes.example: Like a company’s staff register with desks and teams, but machines and apps can query it too.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the concept of directory services and Active Directory, “What is a directory service?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS)?
notes.back: The most widely deployed Active Directory component: it stores users, devices and groups in a domain, verifies sign-in credentials and defines access rights.
notes.explanation: Active Directory is Microsoft’s set of directory services for managing on-premises, domain-based networks.
notes.example: Like the head office register and gatekeeper for every branch on the company’s private network.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the concept of directory services and Active Directory, “Active Directory Domain Services”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In AD DS, what is an organizational unit (OU)?
notes.back: A container used to organise users and computers for simpler administration.
notes.explanation: Organising objects into these units is one of the abilities the unit lists for AD DS.
notes.example: Like folders in a filing cabinet, one per department, holding that department’s staff records.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the concept of directory services and Active Directory, “Active Directory Domain Services”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is federation?
notes.back: Enabling access to services across organisational or domain boundaries by setting up trust relationships between separate identity providers.
notes.explanation: Users can then sign in with their own organisation’s identity provider instead of creating a separate account.
notes.example: Like a library card from your town that neighbouring towns’ libraries agree to accept.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the concept of federation, “Describe the concept of federation”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which perimeter-eroding factor means email and line-of-business apps now run outside the corporate network entirely?
notes.explanation: Business-critical workloads have moved to the cloud.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define identity as the primary security perimeter, “The traditional security perimeter”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which perimeter-eroding factor means a worker’s traffic may never pass through the corporate perimeter at all?
notes.explanation: Employees connect from home networks, public Wi-Fi and locations worldwide.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define identity as the primary security perimeter, “The traditional security perimeter”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which perimeter-eroding factor involves phones and laptops that the organisation does not fully manage or control?
notes.explanation: Employees reach corporate resources on their own phones, tablets and laptops.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define identity as the primary security perimeter, “The traditional security perimeter”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which perimeter-eroding factor involves vendors, contractors and customers who need specific resources without joining the internal network?
notes.explanation: These external users still need access to particular resources.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define identity as the primary security perimeter, “The traditional security perimeter”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which perimeter-eroding factor involves connected devices whose credentials and interfaces are hard to manage with traditional tools?
notes.explanation: They reach organisational networks from facilities and customer locations.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define identity as the primary security perimeter, “The traditional security perimeter”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the unit, what is an identity?
notes.back: The set of attributes that define or characterise a person, a device or a software component.
notes.explanation: A user’s might include username, role, permissions and registered sign-in methods; a device’s its hardware ID and compliance.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define identity as the primary security perimeter, “Identity as the new security perimeter”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: With identity as the perimeter, the security question changes from “Is this request from inside our network?” to what?
notes.back: “Who or what is making this request, and should it be trusted?”
notes.explanation: Every access decision starts with identity.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define identity as the primary security perimeter, “Identity as the new security perimeter”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which type of identity represents employees, contractors, customers and partners?
notes.explanation: They are the people who sign in to use applications and data.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define identity as the primary security perimeter, “Types of identities”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which type of identity can be enrolled in management, checked for compliance and trusted or restricted by its state?
notes.explanation: They represent hardware such as laptops, phones, tablets and IoT sensors.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define identity as the primary security perimeter, “Types of identities”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which type of identity represents applications, services and automated processes that reach resources with no human actively involved?
notes.explanation: They represent software rather than people or hardware.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define identity as the primary security perimeter, “Types of identities”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which type of identity needs purpose-built constructs beyond traditional application identities, to act for users or processes?
notes.explanation: The unit says unmanaged agent identities introduce risks similar to other unmanaged identities.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define identity as the primary security perimeter, “Types of identities”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which identity infrastructure pillar covers provisioning, updating and deprovisioning identities?
notes.explanation: It also includes the policies that govern how identities are managed.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define identity as the primary security perimeter, “Four pillars of an identity infrastructure”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which identity infrastructure pillar challenges an identity for legitimate credentials before access is granted?
notes.explanation: It verifies that the identity is who or what it claims to be.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define identity as the primary security perimeter, “Four pillars of an identity infrastructure”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which identity infrastructure pillar weighs assigned permissions and request context, then grants or restricts access?
notes.explanation: Its goal is that identities reach only what their role or task needs.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define identity as the primary security perimeter, “Four pillars of an identity infrastructure”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which identity infrastructure pillar records who did what, when and from where?
notes.explanation: The unit says it is essential for compliance, detecting incidents and scoping a breach.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define identity as the primary security perimeter, “Four pillars of an identity infrastructure”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A password, a numeric passcode or a security question belongs to which authentication factor category?
notes.explanation: It is one of three categories of proof.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define authentication and authorization, “Authentication”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A mobile device, a hardware security key or a smart card belongs to which authentication factor category?
notes.explanation: It is one of three categories of proof.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define authentication and authorization, “Authentication”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A fingerprint or facial scan belongs to which authentication factor category?
notes.explanation: Biometric characteristics make up this category.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define authentication and authorization, “Authentication”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is single-factor authentication?
notes.back: Signing in with only one factor, such as a password alone.
notes.explanation: If that one factor is compromised, an attacker has everything needed to impersonate the user.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define authentication and authorization, “Authentication”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Multifactor authentication requires two or more factors from {{c1::different categories}}.
notes.explanation: An attacker would then need to compromise several independent credentials.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define authentication and authorization, “Authentication”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Authorisation decisions are typically based on what three things?
notes.explanation: For example a manager role, read or write permission, or a department attribute.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define authentication and authorization, “Authorization”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Authentication happens {{c1::first}}, at sign-in; authorisation happens after it.
notes.explanation: The unit says you cannot decide what someone may do without first confirming who they are.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define authentication and authorization, “How authentication and authorization work together”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A user tries to sign in to an app that uses an identity provider. What happens?
notes.back: The app sends the user to the identity provider, which verifies the credentials and issues a security token the app accepts.
notes.explanation: The application trusts the identity provider, so it accepts the token as proof of authentication.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “The role of the identity provider”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which benefit of a central identity provider lets MFA requirements be applied across all apps from one place?
notes.explanation: Without it, each app may set its own password and MFA standards.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Why centralize authentication?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which benefit of a central identity provider lets suspicious sign-in patterns be spotted across the whole environment?
notes.explanation: Detection then covers every connected app, not just one.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Why centralize authentication?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which benefit of a central identity provider covers provisioning users when they join and deprovisioning them when they leave?
notes.explanation: Without it, administrators must update access in every app separately.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Why centralize authentication?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two kinds of information a token’s claims can include?
notes.back: Any two: unique identifier, display name and email, roles or groups, issue and expiry times, what the token permits.
notes.explanation: Each claim is one piece of data about the authenticated identity.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Security tokens and claims”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why are security tokens time-limited?
notes.back: So that a stolen token cannot be used indefinitely.
notes.explanation: Tokens expire after a set period.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Security tokens and claims”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: OpenID Connect is built on top of {{c1::OAuth 2.0}}.
notes.explanation: The unit gives OpenID Connect for authentication and OAuth 2.0 for authorisation.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Authentication protocols”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which of the three common identity protocols is often used with on-premises identity systems?
notes.explanation: It is common in enterprise scenarios, including older apps and federation.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Authentication protocols”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which SSO benefit means users need not remember separate credentials for each app?
notes.explanation: It is one of three SSO benefits the unit lists.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Single sign-on”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which SSO benefit comes from fewer credential prompts and fewer passwords?
notes.back: Stronger security: fewer chances for phishing or password theft, and less password reuse.
notes.explanation: It is one of three SSO benefits the unit lists.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Single sign-on”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which SSO benefit makes offboarding faster and more reliable?
notes.back: Centralised control: disabling the account in the identity provider removes access to all connected apps.
notes.explanation: It is one of three SSO benefits the unit lists.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Single sign-on”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a server running AD DS called?
notes.explanation: It is where credentials are verified at sign-in.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the concept of directory services and Active Directory, “Active Directory Domain Services”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which AD DS capability lets one user identity work across many on-premises systems?
notes.back: Managing multiple on-premises systems with a single identity per user.
notes.explanation: It is one of four abilities the unit lists for AD DS.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the concept of directory services and Active Directory, “Active Directory Domain Services”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which AD DS feature controls device configurations across the organisation?
notes.explanation: It is one of four abilities the unit lists for AD DS.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the concept of directory services and Active Directory, “Active Directory Domain Services”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is one established protocol AD DS uses to authenticate users to on-premises applications?
notes.back: Kerberos (the unit names two such protocols).
notes.explanation: Modern protocols such as OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, by contrast, are not natively supported by AD DS.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the concept of directory services and Active Directory, “Active Directory Domain Services”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Can AD DS natively authenticate users to SaaS applications?
notes.back: No. It typically needs extra synchronisation tools or federation services.
notes.explanation: AD DS was designed for an on-premises world.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the concept of directory services and Active Directory, “Limitations of Active Directory for a modern environment”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which AD DS limitation concerns iOS and Android?
notes.back: It does not natively manage non-Windows devices without additional solutions.
notes.explanation: It served organisations whose staff used organisation-provided Windows devices.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the concept of directory services and Active Directory, “Limitations of Active Directory for a modern environment”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which two modern authentication protocols does AD DS not natively support?
notes.explanation: Many cloud services and modern apps rely on them.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the concept of directory services and Active Directory, “Limitations of Active Directory for a modern environment”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does a user away from the corporate network need to authenticate directly to AD DS?
notes.explanation: The unit calls this added friction and a potential security gap.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the concept of directory services and Active Directory, “Limitations of Active Directory for a modern environment”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Organisation A’s identity provider trusts Organisation B’s. Does B therefore trust A?
notes.back: No. Trust is not automatically bidirectional; a two-way trust must be explicitly configured.
notes.explanation: Each direction of trust is a separate configuration.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the concept of federation, “How federation works”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In which federation scenario do administrators set a trust between two companies’ identity providers instead of creating guest accounts one by one?
notes.explanation: Partner employees reach shared resources with their own company credentials.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the concept of federation, “Federation in practice”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A consumer app lets people sign in with an existing Google, Microsoft or GitHub account. Is this federation?
notes.back: Yes: a federated sign-in, with the app trusting the social identity provider.
notes.explanation: The unit says this is common in customer-facing apps, where less sign-up friction improves adoption.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the concept of federation, “Federation in practice”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Microsoft server role lets on-premises Active Directory users reach cloud apps by issuing tokens those services accept?
notes.explanation: It extends on-premises authentication to cloud services.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the concept of federation, “Federation in practice”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A sales rep on hotel Wi-Fi opens the company’s SaaS sales app on a personal tablet. What is the main security boundary here?
notes.choices:
A) The office firewall
B) The rep’s identity
C) The hotel’s network
D) The corporate VPN gateway
notes.choicesExplained: A and D sit at a network edge the traffic never crosses. C is not the company’s to control.
notes.explanation: When users and devices connect from outside the network, identity becomes the central point of verification.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define identity as the primary security perimeter, “Identity as the new security perimeter”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A nightly billing job signs in to a database with no person involved. What type of identity does it use?
notes.explanation: Workload identities represent software and automated processes.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define identity as the primary security perimeter, “Types of identities”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: After a breach, investigators trace which accounts signed in and from where. Which identity pillar supports this?
notes.explanation: Auditing records who did what, when and from where, including sign-in logs.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define identity as the primary security perimeter, “Four pillars of an identity infrastructure”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which sign-in combination counts as multifactor authentication?
notes.back: C: a password and a code shown on a hardware key.
notes.choices:
A) A password and a security question
B) A numeric passcode and a memorised phrase
C) A password and a code shown on a hardware key
D) Two different passwords
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D combine two things you know, which is one category.
notes.explanation: Multifactor authentication needs factors from different categories: here something you know and something you have.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define authentication and authorization, “Authentication”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A signed-in contractor can open project files but gets “access denied” when trying to delete them. Which process produced the denial?
notes.choices:
A) Federation
B) Authentication
C) Authorisation
D) Auditing
notes.choicesExplained: A joins identity providers. B already succeeded, since the contractor is signed in. D records activity; it does not decide access.
notes.explanation: Authorisation decides what an authenticated identity may do with each resource.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define authentication and authorization, “Authorization”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A design proposes checking a request’s permissions before confirming who sent it. What is wrong?
notes.back: Authorisation can only happen after successful authentication.
notes.explanation: You cannot tell what someone may do without first confirming their identity.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define authentication and authorization, “How authentication and authorization work together”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A firm’s twenty apps each keep their own accounts, and a leaver kept access to three of them. What would fix this?
notes.choices:
A) Longer passwords in each app
B) A central identity provider that all apps trust
C) A separate firewall per app
D) More administrators
notes.choicesExplained: A does not remove forgotten accounts. C controls traffic, not identities. D still means updating each app separately.
notes.explanation: Central lifecycle management deprovisions a leaver in one place.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Why centralize authentication?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: After sign-in, an app reads the user’s name and unique identifier to show “Welcome back”. Which token does it use?
notes.explanation: The ID token tells the app who the user is.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Security tokens and claims”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A travel app reads a user’s calendar in another service on the user’s behalf. Which token does it present?
notes.explanation: Access tokens grant permission to a specific resource on the user’s behalf.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Security tokens and claims”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A token states that its holder belongs to the Finance group. What is that single statement called?
notes.explanation: Group membership is one of the kinds of claim a token can carry.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Security tokens and claims”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A new mobile banking app must verify who the user is and fetch basic profile details. Which protocol fits?
notes.explanation: It is widely used for authentication in modern cloud and mobile apps.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Authentication protocols”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A printing service needs permission to fetch a user’s photos from their cloud storage. Which protocol grants that access?
notes.explanation: OAuth 2.0 lets apps get access tokens for protected resources on the user’s behalf.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Authentication protocols”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A company needs single sign-on to a long-established enterprise application tied to its on-premises identity system. Which protocol is most likely?
notes.explanation: SAML is common for older enterprise apps and is often used with on-premises identity systems.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Authentication protocols”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An employee leaves. Her account in the identity provider is disabled. What happens to her access to the apps that trust it?
notes.back: It is removed from all of them at once.
notes.explanation: This is the centralised-control benefit of SSO.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Single sign-on”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A company relies only on AD DS. A new remote worker cannot sign in from home. Which AD DS limitation is this?
notes.back: C: no direct authentication without a VPN.
notes.choices:
A) No native support for iOS devices
B) No native SaaS authentication
C) No direct authentication without a VPN
D) No support for OAuth 2.0
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D are real limitations but concern devices, cloud apps and protocols, not working away from the network.
notes.explanation: Users away from the corporate network cannot authenticate directly to AD DS.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the concept of directory services and Active Directory, “Limitations of Active Directory for a modern environment”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Engineers at a supplier must use a manufacturer’s design portal with their own supplier credentials. What should the manufacturer configure?
notes.back: Federation: its identity provider trusts the supplier’s identity provider.
notes.explanation: The manufacturer then accepts the authentication the supplier already performed.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the concept of federation, “How federation works”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A university trusts a hospital’s identity provider. Hospital staff now reach university resources, but university staff cannot reach the hospital’s. Why?
notes.back: B: only a one-way trust was configured.
notes.choices:
A) The hospital’s tokens have expired
B) Only a one-way trust was configured
C) Federation only works within one company
D) Federation needs SAML
notes.choicesExplained: A would stop hospital staff too. C is the opposite of federation’s purpose. D is not the cause: the trust exists and already works in one direction.
notes.explanation: Trust is not automatically bidirectional; a two-way trust must be set up explicitly.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the concept of federation, “How federation works”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Authentication versus authorisation: which question does each answer?
notes.back: Authentication: “Who are you?” Authorisation: “What are you allowed to do?”
notes.explanation: In a building, the first is checking your ID at reception; the second is which doors your pass opens.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define authentication and authorization, “How authentication and authorization work together”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: ID token versus access token: which proves sign-in, and which grants access to a resource?
notes.back: ID token: proves the user signed in (authentication). Access token: grants access to a resource on the user’s behalf (authorisation).
notes.explanation: One tells the app who the user is; the other says what the app may do.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Security tokens and claims”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: OpenID Connect versus OAuth 2.0: which is for authentication and which for authorisation?
notes.explanation: OpenID Connect is built on top of OAuth 2.0.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Authentication protocols”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Single sign-on versus federation: how many identity providers does each involve?
notes.back: SSO can work within one identity provider. Federation is two different identity providers trusting each other across a boundary.
notes.explanation: One sign-in reaching many apps does not by itself mean federation.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the role of the identity provider, “Single sign-on”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: AD DS versus Microsoft Entra ID: what was each designed for?
notes.back: AD DS: on-premises, domain-based networks. Microsoft Entra ID: the internet and the cloud.
notes.explanation: The unit calls Microsoft Entra ID the evolution of directory services for the cloud era.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the concept of directory services and Active Directory, “Microsoft Entra ID”
